analysis.one_liner: Bars dominant online platforms from using their marketplaces to sell their own competing products.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee approved the bill in June 2021, but it never received a vote in the full House or Senate, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forbidden the biggest online platforms — companies like Amazon, Apple, Google, and Meta — from owning businesses that compete on or through their own platforms. It would have covered marketplaces with 50 million or more U.S. monthly users run by companies worth more than $600 billion. In practice, Amazon could not have sold its own private-label goods on Amazon.com, a platform could not force sellers to buy its add-on services, and executives could not sit on boards of spinoff businesses. Violations would have carried fines of up to 15 percent of a company's average daily U.S. revenue.
analysis.who_benefits: Small and mid-sized businesses that sell through dominant platforms, which would no longer have to compete against products the platform itself owns, promotes, or favors. Consumers could gain from more competition, lower prices, and more product choice, and rival retailers and app developers could reach customers without paying a toll to a competitor.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a covered platform from owning or controlling a line of business that sells on the platform — the CRS summary's own example is that Amazon could be barred from selling its private-label products like Amazon Essentials and AmazonBasics on Amazon.com.

Prohibits platforms from offering a product or service a business user must buy as a condition of platform access or preferred placement, so sellers could no longer be pushed to purchase the platform's own advertising, fulfillment, or payment services.

Defines a conflict of interest as platform ownership that lets or incentivizes the operator to advantage its own products or exclude or disadvantage competitors, and bans officers, directors, and employees of a platform from simultaneously serving a formerly affiliated business.

Enforced by the Federal Trade Commission and the Department of Justice with civil penalties up to 15 percent of a company's average daily U.S. revenue, or 30 percent of revenue in the affected line of business, giving the ban real teeth.

analysis.who_pays: The largest online platforms — Amazon most directly — which would have had to divest or spin off private-label product lines and any businesses that compete with their sellers, and would have faced steep fines for noncompliance. Executives and investors in those companies would have borne the loss of revenue from self-preferencing and forced separations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big tech platforms and their executives

drawbacks.text: Structural separation can remove conveniences consumers like: Amazon's fast delivery under Prime is built on the same logistics network that serves its sellers, and Apple's integrated hardware-and-software model is central to its products. Forcing divestitures could raise costs or degrade services for some users.

The 'conflict of interest' standard is broad and fact-specific, which invited litigation and years of court challenges over the D.C. Circuit review the bill provides; businesses would have faced legal uncertainty during designation fights.

The law applies only to platforms with 50 million U.S. users run by companies worth more than $600 billion, so it targets today's giants while leaving other consolidating sectors untouched — a deliberately narrow sweep critics called arbitrary.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is real: breaking the platforms' ability to compete against their own sellers would strengthen small businesses and competition, at the price of some integration benefits consumers currently enjoy and a long court fight over definitions. On balance it was a serious, structurally enforceable antitrust remedy aimed squarely at the most dominant firms, and its cost falls almost entirely on those firms rather than on ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee approved it in June 2021, but House leaders never scheduled a floor vote, the Senate never took it up, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the bill on June 11, 2021, joined by Reps. Lance Gooden (R-TX), David Cicilline (D-RI), Ken Buck (R-CO), and Jerrold Nadler (D-NY), and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day.
It gathered 24 cosponsors — 17 Democrats and 7 Republicans — unusual bipartisan support for a bill targeting the largest tech companies.
The Judiciary Committee held markup sessions on June 23 and 24, 2021, and on June 24 ordered the bill to be reported to the House with amendments.
No further action ever appears in the record: the House never voted on it, the Senate never considered it, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest online platforms. Amazon, Apple, Google, and Meta kept their ability to sell their own products on platforms they control and avoided fines of up to 15 percent of daily U.S. revenue, because House leadership never allowed the bill a vote before the Congress ended.

for.name: Rep. Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 11, 2021, to prohibit dominant platforms from owning businesses that compete on their own platforms.

for.name: Rep. David Cicilline
for.what_they_did: Original introducer of the bill, part of a package of platform-competition bills following a two-year investigation into the tech giants.

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Original introducer; his committee held markups on June 23-24, 2021 and ordered the bill reported with amendments.

for.name: Reps. Ken Buck and Lance Gooden
for.what_they_did: Joined as original introducers, giving the bill Republican backing from the start.

for.name: 17 House Democrats and 7 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, 24 members in total.

for.name: House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Considered and marked up the bill on June 23-24, 2021, and ordered it reported to the House as amended.

against.name: Speaker Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill — or its package of companion platform-competition bills — for a vote on the House floor after the Judiciary Committee approved it in June 2021.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought a Senate version of the platform-conflicts bill to the floor; the chamber never considered the measure at all in 2021 or 2022.

against.name: Amazon, Apple, Google, and Meta
against.what_they_did: Mounted a large-scale lobbying and advertising campaign against the antitrust package, arguing it would break up products consumers liked; Amazon's private-label business was the bill's most direct target.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan in both chambers' pipelines: 17 of 24 cosponsors were Democrats and 7 were Republicans, and the bill was introduced by a mix of two Republicans and three Democrats on the Judiciary Committee — while the decisions that stalled it were made by Democratic House and Senate leadership.

industries.industry: Large online platforms (Amazon, Apple, Google, Meta)
industries.note: The bill would have forced these firms to divest private-label and add-on businesses that compete with their own sellers, and exposed them to fines up to 15 percent of daily U.S. revenue. Their revenue depends partly on self-preferencing their own products against sellers who have no choice of marketplace, so their interest in defeating the bill ran directly against the sellers' and consumers' interest.

industries.industry: Third-party sellers and small businesses on big platforms
industries.note: These businesses would no longer have to compete on a platform they depend on against products the platform itself owns and can favor in search results, or be required to buy the platform's own services to get preferred placement.
The CRS summary names Amazon's private-label goods as the paradigm case the bill would prohibit selling on Amazon.com, eliminating a sales channel built on access the platform controls.
